findings:
  latest: verified — 0 failures. Exercised 24 hand fixtures, all 120 permutations of a tie-free multiset with identical output every time, interleaved multi-sensor cases and 400 seeded randomized cases. readings.py line 36 keeps the largest timestamp per sensor and the per-sensor best dict keeps sensors independent.
  tie: needs_changes — 73 failures. Minimal witness tie_two: [{sensor a, timestamp 1, value 10},{sensor a, timestamp 1, value 20}] returned {a: 10} where acceptance requires {a: 20}. Reverse order tie_two_rev fails symmetrically, returning 20 where 10 is required, so this is the tie rule itself and not one ordering. Also fails tie_three, tie_then_lower, tie_falsy and all six tied permutations. Cause: readings.py line 36 compares with strict timestamp > best[sensor][0], so an equal timestamp never displaces the record already held and the first of a tied group wins. Changing that comparison to >= is sufficient; nothing else in the function needs to move. The docstring at lines 21-24 and the comment at lines 34-35 state this first-wins policy explicitly and acknowledge it diverges from the registered criterion.
  preserve: verified — 0 failures. Empty input returns an empty dict. Every input record was compared against an id-keyed deep copy using a bit-exact, key-order-sensitive comparison, including float, signed-zero, NaN and 2**53+1 fixtures, and none was mutated: the function writes only to its local best dict and builds a fresh dict at line 38. Output key set equals the sensor set exactly and values are the selected records values.
